Latency alarms don’t describe the input data distribution.
Drift checks compare production feature distributions with a baseline from training data.
takeaway: Drift detection starts with a baseline of training data statistics.

question: A team has trained a new version of a fraud model and wants to compare its latency and predictions with the current model on real production traffic, without any customer receiving the new model’s predictions. Which approach should the team use?
options: A canary deployment that shifts 10% of traffic
Batch transform on last month’s data
A SageMaker AI shadow test with the new model as a shadow variant
A/B testing with 50% of traffic sent to the new model
explanations: Canary traffic is served by the new model.
Historical batch data isn’t live production traffic.
Shadow variants receive a copy of production requests, but their responses aren’t returned to callers.
In an A/B test, customers receive responses from the new model.
takeaway: Compare on live traffic with no customer impact → shadow testing.

question: A lender must tell each rejected applicant which factors most influenced their individual decision. Which technique provides these per-prediction explanations?
options: A confusion matrix for the model
Global feature importance from the training run
SHAP values for each prediction
The ROC curve for the model
explanations: A confusion matrix summarizes overall errors, not individual decisions.
Global importance doesn’t explain a single applicant’s result.
SHAP attributes each prediction to the features that pushed it up or down.
ROC curves describe threshold trade-offs across all predictions.
takeaway: Per-prediction explanations → SHAP (local feature attributions).

question: A data science team wants to show business stakeholders how the predicted probability of churn changes, on average, as monthly price increases across all customers. Which explanation technique is designed for this?
options: An AUC comparison between two models
A partial dependence plot (PDP) for monthly price
SHAP values for a single customer
A confusion matrix at several thresholds
explanations: AUC compares model ranking quality.
A PDP shows the average change in predictions as one feature varies.
Single-customer SHAP values explain one prediction, not the average effect.
Confusion matrices don’t show how a feature affects predictions.
takeaway: Average effect of one feature → partial dependence plot.

question: While training a recurrent neural network, the loss suddenly becomes NaN after a few hundred steps. Gradient norms logged by the training script grow very large just before the failure. Which TWO actions should the ML engineer take? (Select TWO.)
options: Remove the activation functions
Apply gradient clipping
Increase the number of epochs
Lower the learning rate
Increase the batch size tenfold and the learning rate tenfold
explanations: Removing non-linearities breaks the model’s ability to learn.
Clipping caps gradient norms and prevents exploding updates.
Training longer doesn’t fix diverging gradients.
Smaller steps reduce the chance of numerical overflow.
A much larger learning rate makes divergence more likely.
takeaway: NaN loss with huge gradients → gradient clipping and a lower learning rate.

question: A model screens medical images for a serious disease. Missing a positive case is far more costly than sending a healthy patient for a follow-up test. Which metric should the team prioritize?
options: Specificity
Recall
Accuracy
Precision
explanations: Specificity measures how well negatives are identified.
Recall measures the share of actual positives the model finds, so it penalizes missed cases.
Accuracy can look high even when rare positives are missed.
Precision focuses on avoiding false positives.
takeaway: Costly false negatives → maximize recall.

question: An email security model moves suspected phishing emails to quarantine. Users complain that legitimate business emails are often quarantined. Which metric should the team improve?
options: Precision
Perplexity
Mean absolute error
Recall
explanations: Precision measures how many quarantined emails are really phishing, so it penalizes false positives.
Perplexity evaluates language models.
MAE is a regression metric.
Recall focuses on catching every phishing email.
takeaway: Costly false positives → improve precision.

question: A delivery time model is evaluated on data that includes occasional extreme delays caused by storms. The business wants a metric that reflects typical errors and isn’t dominated by these rare extremes. Which metric should the team use?
options: R-squared on the training set
F1 score
Root mean squared error (RMSE)
Mean absolute error (MAE)
explanations: Training-set R² doesn’t measure generalization and doesn’t address outliers.
F1 is a classification metric.
Squaring errors makes RMSE sensitive to large outliers.
MAE weights all errors linearly, so rare extremes have less influence.
takeaway: Outlier-robust regression error → MAE; penalize large errors → RMSE.

question: Two binary classifiers will be used with different decision thresholds by different teams. The ML engineer needs a single metric that compares how well each model ranks positives above negatives across all thresholds. Which metric should the engineer use?
options: Mean squared error of the labels
Precision at a threshold of 0.9
Accuracy at a threshold of 0.5
Area under the ROC curve (AUC)
explanations: MSE isn’t the standard ranking metric for classifiers.
Precision also depends on one threshold.
Accuracy depends on one threshold.
AUC summarizes performance across all thresholds.
takeaway: Compare classifiers across thresholds → AUC.

question: A company wants subject-matter experts from its own legal team to rate and compare responses from two Bedrock models for tone and legal soundness, which automated metrics can’t judge reliably. Which solution should the ML engineer use?
options: A CloudWatch dashboard of token counts
An Amazon Rekognition content moderation job
An automatic model evaluation job with the built-in toxicity metric
A Bedrock evaluation job with human workers from its own team
explanations: Token counts don’t measure response quality.
Rekognition moderates images and videos.
Toxicity scores don’t capture legal soundness or tone preferences.
Human-based evaluation jobs let your own experts rate and compare model responses.
takeaway: Subjective expert judgment → Bedrock human-based evaluation with your own team.

question: A team evaluates a model on two tasks: summarizing support tickets and translating them into Spanish. It has reference outputs for both tasks. Which TWO metrics are commonly used for these tasks? (Select TWO.)
options: ROUGE for the summaries
Mean absolute error for both tasks
Word error rate for the summaries
BLEU for the translations
AUC for the translations
explanations: ROUGE measures n-gram overlap with reference summaries, with an emphasis on recall.
MAE is a regression metric.
WER is used for speech recognition transcripts.
BLEU measures n-gram precision against reference translations.
AUC is a classification metric.
takeaway: Summaries → ROUGE; translations → BLEU.

question: A summarization model often produces correct summaries that use different words from the reference summaries, so ROUGE scores are low even when human reviewers rate the summaries highly. Which metric better reflects meaning?
options: Perplexity
Word error rate
BLEU
BERTScore
explanations: Perplexity measures how well a model predicts text, not similarity to a reference.
WER counts word-level edits and penalizes paraphrases.
BLEU is also based on exact n-gram overlap.
BERTScore compares contextual embeddings, so paraphrases with the same meaning score well.
takeaway: Paraphrase-tolerant similarity → BERTScore (embedding-based).

question: A team needs to evaluate 20,000 chatbot responses for correctness, completeness, and helpfulness every week. Human review of all responses is too slow and expensive. Which approach will meet these requirements with the LEAST effort?
options: A Bedrock evaluation job that uses a judge model
Ask the chatbot to grade its own responses inline
Compute BLEU scores for every response
Count the tokens in each response
explanations: An evaluator LLM scores each response on metrics such as correctness, completeness, and helpfulness and explains the score.
Self-grading inside the same call is biased and unstructured.
BLEU needs reference texts and doesn’t judge helpfulness.
Length isn’t a quality measure.
takeaway: Scalable qualitative scoring → LLM-as-a-judge evaluations.

question: Before launch, a company must check whether its Bedrock-based assistant produces stereotypes about demographic groups in its responses. Which evaluation approach should the team use?
options: Compare the training and validation loss curves of the underlying model
Measure ROUGE against reference answers
Run a judge-model evaluation that uses the Stereotyping metric
Run a Glue Data Quality job on the prompts
explanations: Loss curves don’t reveal stereotyping in outputs.
Overlap metrics don’t detect stereotypes.
Bedrock’s Stereotyping metric flags responses that contain stereotypes about groups.
Data quality rules check data structure, not model behavior.
takeaway: Stereotypes in LLM outputs → evaluate with the Stereotyping (responsible AI) metric.

question: A team wants to know whether poor answers from its RAG application come from retrieval or from generation. It has questions with ground-truth passages. Which evaluation should the team run first to isolate retrieval quality?
options: A retrieve-only RAG evaluation job
A latency test of the knowledge base API
A model evaluation job on the generation model without the knowledge base
A human evaluation of the final answers’ tone
explanations: Retrieve-only evaluation scores the retrieved passages, which isolates retrieval problems.
Latency doesn’t measure retrieval accuracy.
This tests the model alone and ignores retrieval.
Tone doesn’t show whether the right passages were retrieved.
takeaway: Isolate retrieval quality → retrieve-only RAG evaluation (context relevance/coverage).

question: A scikit-learn model receives a few hundred requests a day in unpredictable bursts, with hours of no traffic in between. Requests can tolerate an occasional delay of a few seconds. The model needs 2 GB of memory and no GPU. Which deployment option is the MOST cost-effective?
options: SageMaker Serverless Inference
A batch transform job that runs every 10 minutes and waits for new requests
A real-time endpoint on an ml.m5.large instance with auto scaling to two instances
A multi-model endpoint on a GPU instance that hosts the model with other models
explanations: Serverless endpoints scale to zero when idle and bill per use; cold starts are acceptable here.
Batch transform is for offline datasets, not on-demand requests.
Real-time endpoints keep at least one instance running and billing during idle hours.
A GPU instance is unnecessary and runs continuously.
takeaway: Spiky, infrequent, CPU-only traffic that tolerates cold starts → serverless inference.

question: A model analyzes uploaded videos of up to 800 MB, and each analysis takes 10–20 minutes. Users are notified when results are ready. The endpoint should cost nothing when there are no uploads. Which inference option should the ML engineer use?
options: Asynchronous inference with an SNS success notification
Real-time inference with a 60-second timeout
A batch transform job that is started for each uploaded video
Serverless inference with the largest memory size
explanations: Async inference queues requests, accepts payloads up to 1 GB, runs up to an hour, and can scale to zero.
Real-time requests can’t carry 800 MB payloads or run for 20 minutes.
Starting a batch job per upload adds startup delay and doesn’t provide an endpoint queue.
Serverless has small payload limits and short timeouts.
takeaway: Large payloads, long processing, scale to zero → asynchronous inference.

question: Every night, a bank scores 40 million accounts for churn risk and writes the results to Amazon S3. No application needs predictions during the day. Which option is the MOST cost-effective?
options: Asynchronous inference with one request per account
A SageMaker AI batch transform job
Serverless inference with 40 million individual requests
A real-time endpoint that runs all day and is invoked overnight
explanations: Async endpoints are for individual queued requests, not bulk datasets.
Batch transform runs on a full dataset and releases the compute when the job ends.
Per-request invocation of a whole dataset is slow and expensive.
A persistent endpoint bills while idle all day.
takeaway: Score a whole dataset on a schedule → batch transform.

question: A team self-hosts an open-weight 8-billion-parameter model for an interactive assistant that needs time-to-first-token under 300 ms and steady traffic all day. Which deployment option is MOST appropriate?
options: An asynchronous endpoint that sends results to an SNS topic
SageMaker Serverless Inference with 6 GB of memory
A batch transform job that runs every minute on new prompts
A real-time GPU endpoint with an LMI container
explanations: Async inference queues requests and doesn’t suit live chat.
Serverless inference doesn’t support GPUs and has cold starts.
Batch jobs can’t meet interactive latency.
Real-time GPU endpoints with an optimized LMI container serve steady interactive LLM traffic with low latency.
takeaway: Interactive, steady LLM traffic → real-time GPU endpoint (LMI container).

question: A SaaS company trains a separate XGBoost model for each of its 3,000 customers. Each model is small and is called a few times an hour. Hosting one endpoint per model is too expensive. Which solution is the MOST cost-effective?
options: A multi-model endpoint that loads models from Amazon S3 on demand
A multi-container endpoint with 3,000 containers
An inference pipeline that runs all 3,000 models in sequence
One serverless endpoint per customer with provisioned concurrency
explanations: Multi-model endpoints share instances across many same-framework models and cache them on demand.
Multi-container endpoints support up to 15 containers, not thousands.
Pipelines chain containers for one request; they don’t host many alternative models.
Provisioned concurrency on 3,000 endpoints adds a constant cost for each one.
takeaway: Many small, same-framework models with sparse traffic → multi-model endpoint.

question: A team must host a TensorFlow model and a PyTorch model that are invoked independently by different applications. Traffic is low, and the team wants to share one endpoint to reduce cost without modifying the models into one container. Which option should the team use?
options: An inference pipeline that runs the TensorFlow model, then the PyTorch model
A multi-model endpoint with both models
Two production variants with 50% traffic each
A multi-container endpoint with direct invocation of each container
explanations: Pipelines run containers in sequence for every request, which these apps don’t need.
Multi-model endpoints require models that use the same serving container.
Variants split traffic between versions; apps can’t choose a framework per request without extra routing.
Multi-container endpoints host different containers on one endpoint and can invoke each one directly.
takeaway: Different frameworks, independent calls, one endpoint → multi-container endpoint (direct invocation).

question: Every prediction request must pass through a scikit-learn feature transformer, then an XGBoost model, and then a post-processing step that formats the result. The team wants one endpoint call per request. Which deployment pattern fits?
options: A multi-model endpoint that hosts the three artifacts
An asynchronous endpoint with three SNS topics
A SageMaker AI inference pipeline with three containers
Three separate endpoints called one after another by the client
explanations: Multi-model endpoints serve one model per request, not a chain.
Async notifications don’t chain processing steps.
An inference pipeline runs up to 15 containers in sequence behind one endpoint call.
This adds network hops and client complexity.
takeaway: Sequential preprocess → model → postprocess in one call → inference pipeline.

question: A team hosts three fine-tuned open-weight models on SageMaker AI. Each needs a different number of GPUs, and traffic for each model varies independently. The team wants to share instances and scale each model separately. Which feature should the team use?
options: Three production variants with fixed traffic weights
Inference components on a single real-time endpoint
A multi-model endpoint with GPU instances
One serverless endpoint per model
explanations: Variants split one model’s traffic; they don’t isolate resources per model.
Inference components assign accelerators and memory per model and scale each model’s copies independently.
Multi-model endpoints don’t let you allocate GPUs per model or scale models separately.
Serverless inference doesn’t support GPUs.
takeaway: Multiple models sharing GPU instances with per-model resources and scaling → inference components.

question: A company wants to use a foundation model through an API for a document assistant. The team has no infrastructure staff, traffic is unpredictable, and the model is available in Amazon Bedrock. Which deployment option has the LEAST operational overhead?
options: Run the model in Amazon EKS with GPU node groups
Deploy the model from SageMaker JumpStart to a real-time endpoint with auto scaling
Run the model on Amazon EC2 GPU instances behind a load balancer
Invoke the model on demand through the Amazon Bedrock API
explanations: Kubernetes adds significant operational work.
Self-hosting requires choosing instances, scaling policies, and patching containers.
This requires managing servers, drivers, and scaling.
Bedrock is serverless; you pay per token with no infrastructure to manage.
takeaway: Least ops for an available FM → Bedrock on-demand.

question: A team fine-tuned a Llama-architecture model on another platform and has the weights in Hugging Face safetensors format. It wants to serve the model through the same serverless Bedrock APIs that its applications already use. Which solution should the team use?
options: Register the weights in a Bedrock prompt in Prompt Management
Create a Bedrock fine-tuning job that uses the weights as training data
Amazon Bedrock Custom Model Import
Upload the weights to a Bedrock knowledge base
explanations: Prompt Management stores prompts, not models.
Fine-tuning jobs take datasets, not finished weights.
Custom Model Import brings supported open architectures from S3 into Bedrock for serverless invocation.
Knowledge bases store documents for retrieval, not model weights.
takeaway: Bring your own fine-tuned open-weight model to Bedrock APIs → Custom Model Import.

question: A data scientist trained a scikit-learn model on a laptop and saved it as model.joblib. The team wants to host it on a SageMaker AI real-time endpoint without building a container. What should the team do?
options: Convert the model into a Bedrock custom model
Put model.tar.gz in S3 and use the prebuilt scikit-learn container
Retrain the model with the SageMaker AI Linear Learner algorithm
Upload model.joblib to Amazon ECR as a container image and point the endpoint at it
explanations: Bedrock imports supported foundation model architectures, not scikit-learn models.
Prebuilt framework containers load your artifact from S3 and run your inference handler.
Retraining isn’t needed to host an existing model.
ECR stores container images, not model files.
takeaway: Model trained elsewhere → artifact in S3 + prebuilt framework container.

question: A team built an agent with the Strands Agents framework. It must serve many users with complete isolation between user sessions, support sessions that run for up to an hour, and require no servers to manage. Which AWS service should the team use to host the agent?
options: AWS Lambda with a 15-minute timeout
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime
A SageMaker AI real-time endpoint
Amazon EC2 instances in an Auto Scaling group
explanations: Lambda’s 15-minute limit is too short, and session isolation and state must be built yourself.
AgentCore Runtime is serverless, framework-agnostic, isolates each session in its own microVM, and supports long-running sessions.
Endpoints serve model inference, not long-running isolated agent sessions.
EC2 requires managing servers and building session isolation.
takeaway: Serverless, session-isolated hosting for any agent framework → AgentCore Runtime.

question: An agent must call 40 existing internal REST APIs (described with OpenAPI specifications) and several Lambda functions as tools. The team wants the tools exposed through the Model Context Protocol (MCP), with authentication handled centrally. Which service should the team use?
options: AWS Step Functions with one state per API
Amazon EventBridge with one rule per API
Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway
Amazon API Gateway with a usage plan
explanations: Step Functions orchestrates workflows, not agent tool discovery.
EventBridge routes events, not agent tool calls.
AgentCore Gateway converts OpenAPI, Smithy, and Lambda targets into MCP tools and manages inbound and outbound authentication.
API Gateway fronts APIs but doesn’t translate them into MCP tools for agents.
takeaway: Expose APIs and Lambda functions as MCP tools → AgentCore Gateway.

question: A company is building a system in which a planning agent delegates tasks to specialist agents built by other teams, and each agent also calls tools such as databases and search APIs. Which TWO protocols match these interactions? (Select TWO.)
options: OAuth 2.0 for delegating tasks between agents
Agent-to-Agent (A2A) protocol for communication between agents
OpenTelemetry for calling the search and database tools
AG-UI for connecting agents to their tools
Model Context Protocol (MCP) for connecting agents to tools
explanations: OAuth handles authorization; it doesn’t define how agents exchange tasks.
A2A standardizes how agents discover and exchange tasks with other agents.
OpenTelemetry carries traces and metrics, not tool calls.
AG-UI connects agents to user-facing front ends, not to tools.
MCP standardizes how agents discover and call tools and data sources.
takeaway: Agent ↔ agent → A2A; agent ↔ tools → MCP.

topic: Shard a large model across GPUs
question: A 70-billion-parameter model doesn’t fit in the memory of a single GPU on an ml.p4d.24xlarge instance, which has 8 GPUs. The team is deploying it to a SageMaker AI endpoint with a large model inference (LMI) container. Which configuration allows the model to load?
options: Set the number of model copies to 8
Set the tensor parallel degree to 8
Switch to serverless inference with 6 GB of memory
Enable data capture on the endpoint
explanations: Each copy still needs to fit on one GPU.
Tensor parallelism shards the model’s weights across GPUs on the instance.
Serverless inference has no GPUs and far too little memory.
Data capture logs requests; it doesn’t affect memory.
takeaway: Model larger than one GPU at inference → tensor parallelism across GPUs.

question: Users ask a Bedrock knowledge base multi-part questions such as “Compare the parental leave policies in Canada and Japan.” Retrieval returns passages about only one country. Which knowledge base configuration should the ML engineer enable?
options: Query decomposition
A larger chunk overlap
A higher temperature for the generation model
A lower number of retrieved results
explanations: Decomposing the question retrieves passages for each part before generating a combined answer.
Overlap doesn’t help retrieve two separate topics.
Temperature affects generation, not retrieval.
Fewer results make it less likely that both countries are covered.
takeaway: Multi-part questions → query decomposition (reformulation) before retrieval.

question: An application calls a Bedrock model at a steady, high rate around the clock and receives throttling errors during peaks. The business needs guaranteed capacity for the model and can commit to a term. Which option should the ML engineer use?
options: The Flex service tier for every request
Provisioned Throughput for the model
Client retries with exponential backoff
Batch inference for all requests
explanations: Flex trades latency for a discount; it doesn’t guarantee capacity.
Provisioned Throughput reserves dedicated model units for consistent capacity.
Retries help with occasional throttling but don’t add capacity.
Batch inference is asynchronous and doesn’t serve live requests.
takeaway: Steady, high volume needing guaranteed capacity → Provisioned Throughput (commitment).

question: An ML platform team uses AWS CloudFormation. A networking stack creates the VPC, subnets, and security groups, and separate stacks create SageMaker AI endpoints that must use those network resources. How should the endpoint stacks reference the network resources without hard-coding IDs?
options: Store the IDs in a text file in Amazon S3 and download it during deployment
Stack outputs with Export, read with Fn::ImportValue
Create the VPC again in every endpoint stack
Copy the subnet IDs into each endpoint template manually
explanations: This adds custom tooling instead of native stack references.
Stack exports and imports pass values between stacks and keep them consistent.
Duplicating network resources creates separate, unconnected VPCs.
Hard-coded IDs break when the network stack changes.
takeaway: Share values between CloudFormation stacks → Outputs with Export + Fn::ImportValue.

question: An ML team prefers to define its SageMaker AI endpoints, IAM roles, and S3 buckets in Python, using loops and classes, and then deploy them as CloudFormation stacks. Which tool should the team use?
options: AWS CDK
AWS Config
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
AWS CloudTrail
explanations: The CDK defines infrastructure in programming languages such as Python and synthesizes CloudFormation templates.
Config records and evaluates resource configurations.
Parameter Store stores configuration values.
CloudTrail records API activity.
takeaway: Infrastructure defined in Python that deploys through CloudFormation → AWS CDK.

question: A team builds its own inference container for SageMaker AI. Endpoint creation fails with a health check error. Which requirement is the container MOST likely missing?
options: An Application Load Balancer inside the container
Handlers for GET /ping and POST /invocations on port 8080
An SSH server on port 22 so that SageMaker can run health checks
A cron job that downloads the model every minute
explanations: SageMaker provides the endpoint routing.
SageMaker checks health with /ping and sends inference requests to /invocations on port 8080.
SageMaker doesn’t connect to containers over SSH.
SageMaker copies the model artifact to /opt/ml/model at startup.
takeaway: Custom serving containers: /ping and /invocations on port 8080.

question: An ML team pushes inference images to Amazon ECR with the tag “latest.” A rollback failed because the “latest” tag had already been overwritten by a broken image. Which TWO actions will prevent this in the future? (Select TWO.)
options: Delete old images immediately after each push
Store the images in Amazon S3 instead of ECR
Tag each image with a unique version, such as the Git commit ID, and deploy by that tag or digest
Enable enhanced scanning on the repository
Enable tag immutability on the ECR repository
explanations: Deleting old images removes rollback targets.
SageMaker pulls serving images from ECR.
Unique tags or digests make every deployment reproducible and easy to roll back.
Scanning finds vulnerabilities but doesn’t protect tags.
Immutable tags can’t be overwritten by a later push.
takeaway: Reproducible rollbacks → unique image tags/digests + ECR tag immutability.

question: A SageMaker AI endpoint runs in private subnets with no internet access. The model container must read reference data from Amazon S3, and applications in the same VPC must invoke the endpoint without traffic leaving the AWS network. Which TWO resources should the ML engineer create? (Select TWO.)
options: An S3 gateway VPC endpoint
A public IP address on each endpoint instance
An internet gateway attached to the private subnets
A NAT gateway in each private subnet
An interface VPC endpoint for the SageMaker Runtime API
explanations: A gateway endpoint lets resources in private subnets reach S3 without internet access.
Endpoint instances are managed by SageMaker, and public IPs violate the requirement.
This would expose the subnets to the internet.
NAT sends traffic to the internet, which the requirement avoids.
An interface endpoint (PrivateLink) lets applications call InvokeEndpoint privately.
takeaway: Private endpoints: S3 gateway endpoint + SageMaker Runtime interface endpoint.

question: An ML engineer deploys a model to a real-time endpoint by using the low-level Boto3 SageMaker client. In which order must the engineer call the APIs?
options: CreateEndpointConfig, CreateEndpoint, CreateModel
CreateEndpoint, CreateModel, CreateEndpointConfig
CreateModel, CreateEndpointConfig, CreateEndpoint
CreateTrainingJob, CreateEndpoint, CreateModel
explanations: The endpoint configuration must reference an existing model.
An endpoint needs an existing endpoint configuration.
The model defines the container and artifact, the configuration defines the instances, and the endpoint deploys the configuration.
A training job isn’t required to deploy an existing artifact, and the order is wrong.
takeaway: Boto3 deployment: CreateModel → CreateEndpointConfig → CreateEndpoint.

question: A real-time endpoint serves an LLM that streams tokens. Each request runs for 10–40 seconds. Scaling based on InvocationsPerInstance reacts too slowly to traffic spikes, and requests queue up. Which scaling metric should the ML engineer use?
options: CPUUtilization with a target value of 90% on each instance
Invocation4XXErrors
DiskUtilization
The high-resolution ConcurrentRequestsPerModel metric
explanations: GPU-bound LLM serving often shows low CPU even when the model is saturated.
Client errors don’t indicate load.
Disk use doesn’t track concurrent requests.
It counts in-flight requests every 10 seconds, so scaling reacts faster to long-running streaming requests.
takeaway: Long-running or streaming requests → scale on high-resolution concurrent requests.

question: An image generation model on a GPU endpoint saturates the GPU at moderate request rates, but CPU utilization stays low. Which metric should a custom target tracking policy use to scale the endpoint?
options: GPUUtilization
CPUUtilization
Invocation5XXErrors
ModelSetupTime
explanations: Scaling on GPU utilization tracks the resource that limits throughput.
CPU stays low, so the policy wouldn’t scale out.
Errors are a symptom, not a capacity metric to target.
Setup time doesn’t track load.
takeaway: GPU-bound models → scale on GPUUtilization (custom metric).

question: An ML engineer is creating an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for HR documents stored in Amazon S3. Which TWO choices must the engineer make when creating it? (Select TWO.)
options: An Amazon EMR cluster for chunking
An embedding model
A Provisioned Throughput commitment for the embedding model
A vector store, such as Amazon S3 Vectors or OpenSearch Serverless
A SageMaker AI training instance type
explanations: Bedrock handles parsing and chunking during ingestion.
The embedding model converts chunks and queries into vectors.
Embedding calls run on demand by default.
The vector store holds the embeddings for retrieval.
Knowledge bases don’t train models.
takeaway: Knowledge base setup = data source + embedding model + vector store (+ chunking).

question: HR updates documents in the S3 data source of a Bedrock knowledge base several times a day. Employees still receive answers based on old versions. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Increase the number of retrieved results
Switch to a larger embedding model
Run an ingestion job (sync) whenever documents change
Re-create the knowledge base every day from the same S3 data source
explanations: Retrieval still searches the old vectors.
Embedding quality doesn’t fix stale content.
A sync processes added, changed, and deleted documents so the vector store is current.
Re-creating it is unnecessary and disruptive.
takeaway: Changed source documents → run an ingestion job (sync), ideally automated.

question: A team needs full control of the prompt sent to the model: it wants to add retrieved passages, user profile data, and business rules before calling a model of its choice. Which knowledge base API should the application call?
options: The StartIngestionJob API
The InvokeModel API without retrieval
The RetrieveAndGenerate API with default settings
Retrieve, then Converse with its own prompt
explanations: Ingestion jobs sync documents; they don’t answer queries.
Without retrieval, the passages aren’t included.
RetrieveAndGenerate builds the prompt and generates the answer for you, with less control.
Retrieve returns passages so the application can build its own prompt and call any model.
takeaway: Full control of prompt assembly → Retrieve, then call the model yourself.

question: A travel agent built on AgentCore must remember details within a conversation, such as the destination mentioned earlier, and must also remember each user’s seat and meal preferences across future sessions. Which solution meets both requirements with the LEAST custom code?
options: Store the full conversation history in the system prompt of every request
AgentCore Memory (short-term and long-term)
An Amazon ElastiCache cluster with a 5-minute TTL
Model fine-tuning on each user’s conversations every night
explanations: This grows prompts and doesn’t extract preferences across sessions.
Short-term memory keeps turn-by-turn context; long-term memory extracts preferences and facts across sessions.
A short TTL loses preferences between sessions, and extraction must be coded.
Fine-tuning per user is impractical and slow.
takeaway: Within-session context + cross-session preferences → AgentCore Memory (short- and long-term).

question: An agent hosted on AgentCore Runtime must create tickets in a third-party SaaS tool on behalf of each signed-in user, using OAuth tokens. The team doesn’t want to store user tokens in the agent code. Which capability should the team use?
options: Hard-coded API keys in environment variables
IAM roles with a trust policy for the SaaS provider
AWS Secrets Manager with one shared secret for all users
AgentCore Identity for outbound OAuth credential management
explanations: This is insecure and isn’t per user.
IAM roles authorize AWS access, not access to external SaaS APIs.
A shared secret doesn’t act on behalf of each user.
AgentCore Identity handles OAuth flows and securely stores and supplies per-user tokens to the agent.
takeaway: Agents acting on behalf of users in third-party apps → AgentCore Identity (outbound OAuth).

question: A team is deploying a customer service agent that must run serverlessly, call internal APIs as tools, remember customers across sessions, and send traces to CloudWatch. Which combination of AgentCore components meets these requirements?
options: Runtime and Code Interpreter
Code Interpreter, Browser, Policy, and Evaluations
Gateway and Browser
Runtime, Gateway, Memory, and Observability
explanations: This combination lacks API tools and long-term memory.
These provide code execution, web browsing, tool-call authorization, and quality scoring, not hosting, tools, and memory.
There’s no hosting or memory in this combination.
Runtime hosts the agent, Gateway exposes APIs as tools, Memory keeps customer context, and Observability sends traces.
takeaway: Host → Runtime; tools → Gateway; memory → Memory; traces → Observability.

question: A team wants to update a SageMaker AI endpoint to a new model version by first sending 10% of traffic to the new version for 15 minutes and rolling back automatically if latency or error alarms fire. Which deployment configuration should the team use?
options: Delete the endpoint and create a new one with the new model
Add the new model as a second production variant with 0% traffic
A rolling deployment with a batch size of 100%
Blue/green with canary traffic shifting and alarm-based rollback
explanations: This causes downtime and has no rollback.
A 0% variant receives no traffic to test.
This replaces all capacity at once and doesn’t test a canary first.
Canary shifting sends a small share first, bakes, and rolls back if alarms fire.
takeaway: Small first step + bake + automatic rollback → blue/green canary with alarms.

question: A team wants to shift traffic to a new endpoint version in five equal steps of 20%, monitoring alarms after each step. Which traffic shifting mode should the team choose?
options: Shadow
Linear
All at once
Canary
explanations: Shadow testing doesn’t serve the new version’s responses.
Linear shifting moves traffic in equal, configurable steps with baking periods.
All-at-once shifts 100% in one step.
Canary uses two steps: a small canary, then the rest.
takeaway: N equal steps → linear traffic shifting.

question: An endpoint runs on 20 expensive GPU instances. A blue/green update would temporarily require 40 instances, which exceeds the account’s instance quota. The team still wants gradual updates with automatic rollback. Which deployment option should the team use?
options: Blue/green with all-at-once traffic shifting
A rolling deployment in 25% batches with CloudWatch alarms
A multi-model endpoint that loads the new model version on demand
Shadow testing for every update
explanations: Blue/green still provisions a full green fleet.
Rolling deployments update capacity in batches, so they don’t double the fleet, and they can roll back on alarms.
Multi-model endpoints don’t change how updates are rolled out.
Shadow tests evaluate a variant; they don’t replace the production model.
takeaway: Avoid doubling capacity during updates → rolling deployment.

question: An ML team stores its training code in GitHub. On every merge to the main branch, it wants AWS to run unit tests, build a container image, and push it to Amazon ECR. Which combination of services should the team use?
options: Amazon EventBridge with an Amazon SQS queue
AWS CodeArtifact with a scheduled AWS Lambda function
AWS CodePipeline with an AWS CodeConnections source and an AWS CodeBuild stage
AWS CodeDeploy triggered by an Amazon S3 event
explanations: Event routing alone doesn’t build or test code.
CodeArtifact stores packages; it doesn’t run builds.
CodeConnections links GitHub to CodePipeline, and CodeBuild runs tests and builds and pushes the image.
CodeDeploy deploys applications; it doesn’t build images from GitHub merges.
takeaway: GitHub → CodeConnections → CodePipeline → CodeBuild (tests, image build, push).

question: A CodeBuild project builds an inference image successfully but fails at the docker push step with an “AccessDenied” error for Amazon ECR. What should the ML engineer fix?
options: Increase the compute type of the CodeBuild project
Enable privileged mode on the CodeBuild project
Add ECR push permissions to the CodeBuild service role
Move the buildspec file to the repository root and rename it buildspec.yml
explanations: Compute size doesn’t affect ECR permissions.
Privileged mode is needed to build Docker images, and the build already works, so it isn’t the cause.
The service role must allow authenticating to ECR and uploading image layers.
The buildspec already runs; the failure is an authorization error.
takeaway: CodeBuild AccessDenied on ECR → fix the CodeBuild service role permissions.

question: A new training job that uses ml.p4d.24xlarge fails immediately with a ResourceLimitExceeded error. Other training jobs that use ml.m5.xlarge run normally. What should the ML engineer do?
options: Enable managed spot training
Add a VPC configuration with private subnets to the training job
Lower the max_run value of the job
Request a quota increase for ml.p4d.24xlarge training
explanations: Spot training still needs available quota for the instance type.
Networking doesn’t affect instance quotas.
The run time isn’t the limiting factor.
Each instance type has a per-account quota, which can be 0 until you request an increase.
takeaway: ResourceLimitExceeded for an instance type → raise that SageMaker quota.

question: A SageMaker Pipelines workflow trains and evaluates a model each week. The team wants the pipeline to register the model only if its F1 score on the test set is at least 0.85; otherwise, it should stop with a failure message. Which steps should the team add?
options: A Transform step that scores the test set again
A Lambda step that deletes models with low scores after registration
A Callback step that waits for manual review of every model
A Condition step that compares the F1 score, followed by a model registration step or a Fail step
explanations: Scoring again doesn’t decide whether to register.
Registering first and deleting later isn’t a gate.
Manual review isn’t needed for a numeric threshold.
Condition steps branch on evaluation metrics, so only passing models are registered.
takeaway: Metric threshold gate in Pipelines → Condition step → register or Fail.

question: A team wants its SageMaker AI retraining pipeline to start automatically every Sunday and also whenever a drift-detection job publishes a CloudWatch alarm in the ALARM state. Which solution will meet these requirements with the LEAST custom code?
options: An AWS Glue trigger that runs the pipeline
A SageMaker Studio notebook that a team member runs on Sundays
A cron job on an EC2 instance that polls CloudWatch every minute
EventBridge schedule and alarm rules that start the pipeline
explanations: Glue triggers start Glue jobs and crawlers, not SageMaker pipelines.
Manual runs aren’t automated.
This requires managing a server and polling code.
EventBridge can start a SageMaker pipeline directly from schedules and from CloudWatch alarm events.
takeaway: Scheduled or event-driven retraining → EventBridge rules that start the pipeline.

question: Models are registered in SageMaker Model Registry with the status PendingManualApproval. When a reviewer changes a model’s status to Approved, a deployment pipeline must start automatically. How should the ML engineer implement this?
options: Poll the model registry every hour with a Lambda function
An EventBridge rule on the model package state change event
Use an S3 event notification on the model artifact
Ask reviewers to start the deployment manually after approval
explanations: Polling adds delay and custom code.
Model Registry emits events when approval status changes, which EventBridge can route to CodePipeline or a pipeline.
The artifact doesn’t change when the approval status does.
Manual starts aren’t automated.
takeaway: Approval in Model Registry → EventBridge event → deployment pipeline.

question: Auditors ask which training data, code version, and metrics produced each model that was deployed in the last year, and who approved it. Which approach meets this requirement?
options: Register each version in SageMaker Model Registry
Keep the latest model artifact in S3 and overwrite older ones
Store a spreadsheet of model versions in Amazon S3
Use CloudWatch Logs retention of 30 days
explanations: Model Registry versions models in groups and records metrics, lineage, and approval history.
Older versions would be lost.
Manual records are error-prone and aren’t linked to artifacts.
Logs expire and don’t describe model lineage.
takeaway: Model versioning for audits → Model Registry (versions, metrics, lineage, approvals).

question: Developers iterate on a prompt in Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management. Production applications must keep using a tested prompt until a new one is approved. How should the applications reference the prompt?
options: By the prompt name in an environment variable that developers edit
By the ARN of a specific prompt version
By copying the prompt text into the application code
By the prompt’s draft identifier
explanations: Editing a name doesn’t pin a tested version.
Prompt versions are immutable snapshots, so production stays on the tested prompt.
Copies drift from the managed prompt and need code deploys to change.
The draft changes as developers edit it.
takeaway: Pin production to an immutable prompt version.

question: A team deploys an agent with AgentCore Runtime. Every code update creates a new runtime version. Production traffic must stay on the tested version until the team explicitly promotes the next one. How should the team configure production?
options: Pin a production endpoint to a version; update it to promote
Redeploy the agent as a new runtime for each release
Point production clients at the DEFAULT endpoint of the agent runtime
Delete old versions after each update
explanations: Custom endpoints stay on their version until you update them explicitly.
This changes the runtime identity instead of using versions and endpoints.
DEFAULT moves to the latest version automatically after every update.
Versions are immutable and are the rollback targets.
takeaway: AgentCore: DEFAULT tracks latest; pin prod with a named endpoint on a version.

question: Before promoting a new prompt version to production, a team wants its CI/CD pipeline to check automatically that answers to 300 golden questions haven’t become less correct. Which approach should the team add to the pipeline?
options: A manual review of five random answers
A CodeBuild step that checks the prompt for spelling errors
Run a Bedrock evaluation on the golden set and fail below a threshold
A load test that measures latency and throttling at peak production traffic
explanations: A small manual sample isn’t automated or thorough.
Spelling checks don’t measure answer quality.
Automated evaluation against a fixed test set catches regressions before promotion.
Latency tests don’t measure correctness.
takeaway: Prompt CI → automated evaluation on a golden set with a pass/fail threshold.

question: Documents for a Bedrock knowledge base are produced by a nightly ETL job. The team wants the knowledge base to sync only after the ETL job succeeds, and to notify the team if the sync fails. Which solution will meet these requirements?
options: Configure S3 Lifecycle rules on the data source bucket
Ask users to report when answers look outdated
A Step Functions workflow: ETL job, then sync, with an SNS alert on failure
Run the ingestion job on a fixed schedule one hour after the ETL job starts
explanations: Lifecycle rules move or expire objects; they don’t sync knowledge bases.
This isn’t automated.
Step Functions sequences the steps, waits for success, and handles failures.
A fixed schedule can sync before the ETL job finishes.
takeaway: Sequenced data refresh with error handling → Step Functions orchestration.

question: A SageMaker Pipelines workflow reruns a 2-hour data processing step even when its inputs and code haven’t changed, which delays experiments. Which feature should the ML engineer enable?
options: Step caching for the processing step
Managed spot training for the processing step
A Callback step before the processing step
Warm pools for the training step
explanations: Caching reuses a previous successful run when the step’s inputs and configuration are unchanged.
Spot capacity lowers cost but still reruns the step.
Callbacks wait for external signals.
Warm pools reduce startup time for training jobs, not processing reruns.
takeaway: Avoid rerunning unchanged steps → Pipelines step caching.

question: A company already runs hundreds of Apache Airflow DAGs for data engineering and wants to add ML training and deployment tasks to the same DAGs with minimal change to its tooling. Which service should it use?
options: SageMaker Pipelines
Amazon MWAA
AWS Glue workflows
Amazon EventBridge Scheduler
explanations: Pipelines is ML-native but would introduce a second orchestration tool.
MWAA runs existing Airflow DAGs as a managed service, and Airflow has SageMaker operators.
Glue workflows orchestrate Glue jobs and crawlers.
Scheduler starts targets on a schedule but doesn’t run DAGs.
takeaway: Existing Airflow DAGs → Amazon MWAA.

question: An ML engineer runs dozens of short SageMaker AI training jobs in a row while adjusting code. Each job spends several minutes provisioning instances and pulling the container before training starts. Which feature will reduce this startup time for consecutive jobs?
options: A larger instance type for every training job in the series
Managed spot training with a long maximum wait time
SageMaker AI managed warm pools with a keep-alive period
Pipe input mode for all training channels
explanations: Bigger instances don’t remove provisioning time.
Spot capacity lowers cost but can add waiting time.
Warm pools keep instances provisioned after a job ends so the next matching job starts faster.
Pipe mode changes data loading, not instance provisioning.
takeaway: Many back-to-back training jobs → warm pools (KeepAlivePeriodInSeconds).

question: A company runs several applications that call Amazon Bedrock models. The operations team wants a single prebuilt view of invocation counts, latency, token usage, and errors per model, plus traces for agents, without building dashboards by hand. Which solution should the team use?
options: AWS CloudTrail Lake queries over the Bedrock management events
AWS Trusted Advisor checks for the Bedrock service quotas
Amazon Inspector findings for the applications that call Bedrock
Amazon CloudWatch generative AI observability
explanations: CloudTrail records API activity for auditing; it doesn’t chart latency or token usage.
Trusted Advisor gives best-practice recommendations, not invocation dashboards.
Inspector reports software vulnerabilities.
It provides out-of-the-box dashboards for model invocations and AgentCore agents, including latency, tokens, and errors.
takeaway: Prebuilt GenAI dashboards (tokens, latency, errors, agent traces) → CloudWatch generative AI observability.

question: For quality reviews and audits, a company must keep a record of every prompt sent to Amazon Bedrock and every response, along with the model ID and token counts. Which feature should the ML engineer enable?
options: Bedrock model invocation logging to CloudWatch Logs or Amazon S3
AWS CloudTrail management events for Bedrock
Amazon Macie for the Bedrock service
VPC Flow Logs for the subnets that the applications use to call Bedrock
explanations: Invocation logging records request and response data, metadata, and token counts for each call.
Management events record control-plane calls, not prompt and response content.
Macie scans S3 data for sensitive information; it doesn’t capture invocations.
Flow logs capture network metadata, not request bodies.
takeaway: Record prompts and responses → Bedrock model invocation logging.

question: A real-time SageMaker AI endpoint has data capture enabled. The team wants a weekly check that compares production input distributions with a training baseline, records the drift scores alongside the model’s training runs, and alerts the team when drift exceeds a threshold. The account can’t onboard SageMaker Model Monitor. Which design meets these requirements?
options: A weekly Amazon Athena query that counts captured requests
A CloudWatch alarm on the endpoint’s Invocations metric with anomaly detection enabled
An AWS Config rule that evaluates the endpoint configuration and data capture settings weekly
A scheduled job that computes drift (such as PSI), logs to MLflow, and alarms in CloudWatch
explanations: Counts don’t compare distributions with a baseline.
Request volume doesn’t measure changes in input distributions.
Config checks resource settings, not data distributions.
This is AWS’s recommended replacement pattern: compute drift on captured data, track it in MLflow, and alarm through CloudWatch.
takeaway: Drift detection pipeline: captured data vs baseline → drift metrics (PSI/KS) → MLflow + CloudWatch alarm.

question: A team that already uses SageMaker Model Monitor sees stable input distributions, but the features that drive its credit model’s predictions have shifted: a postcode feature now dominates. Which type of monitoring detects this change?
options: Bias drift monitoring
Data quality monitoring with constraints
Feature attribution drift monitoring
Model quality monitoring with ground truth
explanations: Bias drift tracks fairness metrics between groups, not overall feature importance.
Data quality monitoring checks input statistics and constraints, which are stable here.
Feature attribution drift compares current feature importance (SHAP) with the baseline.
Model quality compares predictions with ground truth labels.
takeaway: Changing feature importance → feature attribution drift. (Model Monitor is closed to new customers since July 2026; existing users keep it.)

question: A team wants to track the precision and recall of a deployed fraud model over time. Fraud labels are confirmed by investigators about 30 days after each transaction. What must the monitoring solution include?
options: A baseline computed from the training data’s feature statistics
A CloudWatch alarm on endpoint latency
A smaller decision threshold for the model
Joining delayed ground truth labels to captured predictions
explanations: Feature baselines detect data drift, not precision and recall.
Latency doesn’t measure prediction quality.
Changing the threshold doesn’t provide labels for monitoring.
Model quality metrics require ground truth, which must be matched to the original predictions.
takeaway: Model quality monitoring = predictions + (delayed) ground truth labels.

question: An ML team’s nightly SageMaker Pipelines execution sometimes fails, and nobody notices until the next morning. The team wants an email as soon as an execution fails. Which solution will meet this requirement with the LEAST effort?
options: A daily AWS Budgets report
An EventBridge rule on Failed executions with an SNS email target
A Lambda function that polls the pipeline status every 5 minutes
An AWS Config rule for the pipeline resource
explanations: Budgets track costs, not pipeline failures.
SageMaker emits execution status events that EventBridge can route to SNS immediately.
Polling requires custom code and adds delay.
Config tracks configuration changes, not execution status.
takeaway: Workflow failure alerts → EventBridge status-change rule → SNS.

question: A daily AWS Glue job feeds a model’s feature store. Occasionally an upstream system sends far fewer records than usual, and the job still succeeds. The team wants an alert when the record count is unusually low, without setting a fixed threshold, because volumes vary by weekday. Which solution should the team use?
options: An S3 Lifecycle rule that expires incomplete output files in the bucket
A custom metric for the record count with an anomaly detection alarm
A static CloudWatch alarm with a threshold of 1,000 records
AWS CloudTrail Insights for the Glue API calls
explanations: Lifecycle rules manage object storage classes and expiration.
Anomaly detection learns the expected pattern, including weekly seasonality, and alarms on unusual values.
A fixed threshold can’t follow weekday patterns.
CloudTrail Insights detects unusual API call rates, not data volumes.
takeaway: Unusual values with seasonal patterns → CloudWatch anomaly detection alarms.

question: A team wants to send 10% of live traffic to a new model and 90% to the current model on the same endpoint, and then compare business metrics for each model. Which approach should the team use?
options: Shadow testing with the new model as a shadow variant
Two separate endpoints selected randomly by the client
A batch transform job for the new model on yesterday’s data
Two production variants with weights of 0.1 and 0.9
explanations: Shadow variants don’t return responses to users, so business outcomes can’t be compared.
This works but needs custom routing that variants provide natively.
Offline scoring doesn’t measure live business impact.
Production variants split live traffic by weight, and CloudWatch reports metrics per variant.
takeaway: Live A/B test on one endpoint → production variants with traffic weights.

question: During an A/B test, QA engineers must send specific test requests to the new variant, regardless of the configured traffic weights. How can they do this?
options: Set the TargetVariant parameter in the InvokeEndpoint request
Create a second endpoint configuration for each test
Enable data capture on the new variant and replay the captured requests
Temporarily set the new variant’s weight to 100%
explanations: TargetVariant routes an individual request to a named production variant.
This is unnecessary for routing individual requests.
Data capture records requests; it doesn’t route them.
This would send all users to the new variant.
takeaway: Route one request to a chosen variant → TargetVariant in InvokeEndpoint.

question: A multi-step agent hosted on AgentCore Runtime sometimes gives incomplete answers. The team suspects that one of its tools fails intermittently and that the agent continues anyway. How can the team find which step fails and how often?
options: Inspect tool calls and errors in AgentCore Observability traces
Increase the model’s maxTokens setting
Enable S3 server access logging on the agent’s bucket
Review the AWS Cost Explorer report for the agent’s daily token spend
explanations: Agent traces show each reasoning step, tool invocation, latency, and error.
Output length doesn’t reveal failing tool calls.
S3 logs don’t trace agent reasoning or tool calls.
Costs don’t show step-level failures.
takeaway: Find failing agent steps or tools → AgentCore Observability traces.

question: Users report that some answers from a Bedrock-based assistant stop mid-sentence. The application uses the ConverseStream API. Which approach detects these cases automatically?
options: Enable cross-Region inference
Alarm on the InvocationThrottles metric for the model
Track how often stopReason is max_tokens and alarm on it
Alarm on InputTokenCount when prompts exceed 4,000 tokens
explanations: Routing across Regions doesn’t affect the output limit.
Throttling rejects requests; it doesn’t cut off completed responses.
A stopReason of max_tokens shows that output hit the token limit and was truncated.
Input size doesn’t indicate whether the output was cut off.
takeaway: Truncated output → stopReason = max_tokens; monitor it and raise maxTokens or shorten outputs.

question: A company wants to know whether the answer quality of its Bedrock application declines over time as user questions change. Which approach provides a recurring quality signal with the LEAST manual effort?
options: Ask every user to rate every answer before continuing
Weekly judge-model evaluations on sampled production traffic
Retrain the model every week regardless of results
Track the average InvocationLatency metric for the model each week
explanations: Mandatory ratings hurt the user experience and give sparse, biased data.
Scheduled LLM-as-a-judge evaluations on real traffic produce trend data on quality.
Retraining without measurement doesn’t show whether quality declined.
Latency doesn’t measure answer quality.
takeaway: Recurring FM quality signal → scheduled evaluations (LLM-as-a-judge) on sampled traffic.

question: A company serves a transformer model on GPU instances with steady traffic. It wants to lower inference cost per request while keeping latency similar, and it can compile the model with the AWS Neuron SDK. Which instance family should it evaluate?
options: ml.r5 (memory-optimized CPUs)
ml.p5 (NVIDIA H100 GPUs)
ml.t3 (burstable)
ml.inf2 (AWS Inferentia2)
explanations: R5 instances are memory-optimized CPUs without ML accelerators.
P5 instances target large-scale training and are among the most expensive.
T3 instances are burstable CPUs for light workloads such as notebooks.
Inf2 instances use AWS Inferentia2 chips built for low-cost, high-throughput inference.
takeaway: Cheaper deep learning inference → Inferentia (ml.inf2); cheaper training → Trainium (ml.trn).

question: A small XGBoost model needs about 2 ms of compute per request and receives steady traffic. It currently runs on an ml.g5.xlarge GPU instance with low GPU utilization. Which change will MOST reduce cost?
options: Move to a compute-optimized CPU instance such as ml.c7g or ml.c6i
Move to an ml.p4d.24xlarge instance
Move to an ml.inf2 instance without compiling the model
Add a second GPU instance in another Availability Zone for resilience
explanations: Tree models run efficiently on CPUs, which cost much less than idle GPUs.
A larger GPU instance increases cost.
Inferentia requires Neuron-compiled models and doesn’t suit XGBoost.
This doubles the GPU cost.
takeaway: Lightweight CPU-friendly models → compute-optimized CPU instances, not GPUs.

question: A team trains large language models for weeks at a time and wants to reduce training cost per job compared with GPU instances, using the AWS Neuron SDK. Which instance family is designed for this?
options: ml.c7i (compute-optimized Intel CPUs)
ml.trn1 or ml.trn2 (AWS Trainium)
ml.inf2 (AWS Inferentia2)
ml.t3 burstable instances
explanations: CPUs train large language models far too slowly.
Trainium instances are purpose-built for cost-efficient deep learning training.
Inferentia is optimized for inference.
Burstable instances suit notebooks, not large-scale training.
takeaway: Training cost on AWS silicon → Trainium; inference → Inferentia.

question: An endpoint’s end-to-end latency has doubled. The ML engineer needs to know whether the time is spent inside the model container or in SageMaker AI request handling. Which TWO CloudWatch metrics should the engineer compare? (Select TWO.)
options: InvocationsPerInstance
DiskUtilization
ModelLatency
Invocation4XXErrors
OverheadLatency
explanations: This shows load per instance, not the latency breakdown.
Disk use doesn’t break down request latency.
ModelLatency measures the time the model container takes to respond.
Client errors don’t show where time is spent.
OverheadLatency measures time added by SageMaker outside the container.
takeaway: Latency breakdown → ModelLatency (container) vs OverheadLatency (SageMaker).

question: A RAG application runs as Lambda functions behind API Gateway and calls a knowledge base and a Bedrock model. Some requests take 12 seconds. The team needs an end-to-end view of time spent in each downstream call. Which service should the team use?
options: AWS Config
Amazon Inspector
AWS X-Ray traces
AWS Trusted Advisor
explanations: Config records configuration changes.
Inspector finds vulnerabilities.
Distributed tracing shows the time spent in each service call along the request path.
Trusted Advisor gives account-level best-practice checks.
takeaway: Per-hop latency in distributed requests → X-Ray traces.

question: An ML operations team wants one screen that shows endpoint invocations, model latency, Bedrock token usage, and pipeline failures, with alarms highlighted. Which service should the team use?
options: Amazon Athena
AWS Systems Manager Parameter Store
Amazon CloudWatch dashboards
AWS Cost Explorer
explanations: Athena runs SQL queries on data in S3.
Parameter Store holds configuration values.
Dashboards combine metrics and alarms from many services on one screen.
Cost Explorer shows costs, not operational metrics.
takeaway: One screen of metrics and alarms → CloudWatch dashboards.

question: A business-critical real-time endpoint runs on one ml.c6i.xlarge instance. During an Availability Zone issue, the endpoint was unavailable. Which change will improve availability with the LEAST effort?
options: Enable data capture
Create a second endpoint in the same subnet
Change to a larger instance type
Set the initial instance count to at least two
explanations: Data capture records requests; it doesn’t add redundancy.
This adds complexity and keeps both in one Availability Zone.
A single larger instance is still a single point of failure.
With two or more instances, SageMaker distributes them across Availability Zones.
takeaway: Endpoint HA → two or more instances (spread across AZs).

question: Before launch, a team wants to know which instance type and count will meet a latency target of 100 ms at 500 requests per second at the lowest cost. Which SageMaker AI capability should the team use?
options: SageMaker Inference Recommender
SageMaker Pipelines step caching
SageMaker Feature Store
SageMaker Model Registry
explanations: Inference Recommender runs load tests across instance types and recommends cost-effective configurations.
Caching skips repeated steps.
Feature Store manages features.
The registry versions models; it doesn’t load test instances.
takeaway: Pick an instance type and count against latency/throughput targets → Inference Recommender.

question: An ML team’s monthly spend must not exceed $8,000. The finance team wants email alerts at 80% of forecasted spend and wants the team’s ability to start new SageMaker AI resources restricted automatically when actual spend reaches 100%. Which solution meets these requirements?
options: AWS Cost Explorer saved reports sent daily
AWS Trusted Advisor cost optimization checks with weekly email reports
A CloudWatch billing alarm on the EstimatedCharges metric
AWS Budgets alerts with a budget action that applies a policy
explanations: Reports show costs but don’t alert on thresholds or act.
Trusted Advisor recommends savings but doesn’t enforce limits.
This can alert but can’t apply IAM restrictions.
Budgets alert on forecasted or actual spend, and budget actions can attach restrictive policies.
takeaway: Alerts + automatic enforcement on spend → Budgets with budget actions.

question: Three teams call the same Bedrock foundation model on demand from one AWS account. Finance needs each team’s model usage costs in Cost Explorer. What should the ML engineer do?
options: A tagged application inference profile for each team
Use a different AWS Region for each team
Turn on model invocation logging and sum the tokens in a spreadsheet
Add a team name to each prompt
explanations: Tagged application inference profiles let Cost Explorer split on-demand model costs by tag.
Regions don’t identify teams in cost reports and may lack the model.
This is manual and doesn’t produce billing allocations.
Prompt text doesn’t appear in billing data.
takeaway: Split on-demand Bedrock costs by team/app → tagged application inference profiles.

question: A company runs SageMaker AI real-time endpoints, training jobs, and Studio notebooks with a steady baseline of usage, and it expects to keep that usage for at least a year. The instance types will change as models evolve. Which purchasing option will reduce cost the MOST?
options: A SageMaker AI Savings Plan with a 1-year term
EC2 Reserved Instances for the endpoint instances
On-Demand pricing with a larger instance count
Spot capacity for the real-time endpoints
explanations: SageMaker Savings Plans discount eligible usage across instance families, sizes, and Regions in exchange for a commitment.
EC2 Reserved Instances don’t apply to SageMaker AI usage.
More instances increase cost.
Real-time endpoints don’t run on Spot capacity.
takeaway: Steady SageMaker usage with changing instance types → SageMaker AI Savings Plans.

question: A company must summarize 2 million archived documents with a Bedrock model. Results are needed within a few days, not in real time. Which option will reduce cost the MOST?
options: Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment
On-demand invocation in a tight loop from an EC2 instance
Bedrock batch inference with the prompts in Amazon S3
The Priority service tier for all requests
explanations: A long commitment for a one-time job is expensive.
This pays full on-demand prices and risks throttling.
Batch inference processes large prompt sets asynchronously at a lower price than on-demand.
Priority costs more in exchange for faster responses.
takeaway: Large offline FM jobs → Bedrock batch inference (discounted).

question: A team bought Provisioned Throughput for a base model six months ago. Monitoring now shows that average utilization is under 10%, and traffic is spiky but low. What should the team do when the commitment ends?
options: Buy additional model units to handle the spikes
Move the workload to on-demand inference
Switch to batch inference for the interactive traffic
Renew the commitment for a longer term to get a lower hourly price
explanations: More units raise cost further.
Low, spiky traffic is cheaper on pay-per-token on-demand pricing.
Batch inference doesn’t serve interactive requests.
A cheaper rate on mostly idle capacity still wastes money.
takeaway: Low or spiky FM traffic → on-demand tokens, not idle provisioned capacity.

question: An agent’s monthly cost tripled although the number of user sessions stayed flat. Which metric is the MOST useful first check?
options: The number of CloudTrail management events per day
The S3 storage used by the agent’s code bundle
The number of IAM roles in the account
Tokens and tool calls per session
explanations: Management events don’t explain per-session model and tool usage.
Code storage is a negligible cost.
IAM roles don’t affect usage costs.
More tokens or tool loops per session raise cost even with flat session counts.
takeaway: Agent cost growth with flat sessions → check tokens and tool calls per session (loops, long context).

question: Every request to a Bedrock-based assistant includes the same 30,000-token policy manual followed by a short user question. Costs and latency are high. Which feature will reduce both with the LEAST change?
options: Global cross-Region inference
Prompt caching
Batch inference
A higher maxTokens value
explanations: It offers a modest discount but still reprocesses the full manual on every call.
Cached prompt prefixes are read at a reduced price and processed faster on later calls.
Batch inference is asynchronous and doesn’t suit an interactive assistant.
This affects output length and can increase cost.
takeaway: Same long prefix on many calls → prompt caching.

question: Most questions to a support assistant are simple, but some need a more capable model. The team wants Bedrock to choose between a smaller and a larger model in the same family for each request, to reduce cost without building a classifier. Which feature should the team use?
options: Provisioned Throughput
Model distillation
Intelligent prompt routing
A knowledge base with reranking
explanations: Provisioned Throughput reserves capacity for one model.
Distillation creates a smaller custom model; it doesn’t route requests.
A prompt router predicts which model can answer each prompt well and routes to the cheaper one when possible.
Reranking orders retrieved passages.
takeaway: Per-request choice between models in a family → intelligent prompt routing.

question: A chatbot sends the full conversation history with every request, and long sessions are consuming many input tokens. Which TWO changes will reduce token usage with little impact on quality? (Select TWO.)
options: Send the history as a base64-encoded string
Set maxTokens to fit the expected answer length
Summarize older turns and send the summary with the recent turns
Increase the temperature
Repeat the system prompt twice for emphasis
explanations: Encoding makes the input longer.
A sensible output limit prevents unnecessarily long responses.
A rolling summary keeps context while shrinking the history.
Temperature doesn’t change token counts in a predictable way.
Repetition adds tokens.
takeaway: Token optimization → trim or summarize history, concise prompts, sensible maxTokens.

question: A knowledge base is rebuilt every night by deleting the vector index and re-embedding all 2 million documents, although fewer than 1% change daily. Which change will MOST reduce embedding costs?
options: Increase the chunk overlap
Run the rebuild twice a day
Incremental syncs that skip unchanged documents
Switch to an embedding model with more dimensions
explanations: More overlap creates more text to embed.
This doubles the cost.
Knowledge base ingestion jobs detect changes, so unchanged documents aren’t re-embedded.
Larger embeddings don’t reduce the number of embedding calls.
takeaway: Avoid re-embedding unchanged content → incremental sync.

question: A company stores 1 billion 1,024-dimension vectors in an OpenSearch Service domain for a RAG archive that is queried a few hundred times a day with relaxed latency needs. Storage and cluster costs are high. Which TWO changes will reduce cost? (Select TWO.)
options: Store a second copy of each vector for faster queries
Move the vectors to an in-memory cache
Use smaller embedding dimensions, such as 256, if retrieval tests show acceptable recall
Move the archive vectors to Amazon S3 Vectors
Add more data nodes to the OpenSearch domain
explanations: Duplicates double storage.
Memory is the most expensive tier for rarely queried vectors.
Fewer dimensions shrink storage and compute per vector.
S3 Vectors provides low-cost, serverless storage and querying for large, infrequently used vector sets.
More nodes increase cost.
takeaway: Vector storage cost → S3 Vectors for cold, large sets; fewer dimensions.

question: Cost Explorer shows that SageMaker Studio JupyterLab spaces on GPU instances run overnight and on weekends with no activity. Which change will reduce this cost with the LEAST effort?
options: Delete the SageMaker AI domain every evening
Switch all spaces to GPU instances with more memory
Ask users to email the platform team before they log off each day
Configure idle shutdown for the JupyterLab applications
explanations: Deleting the domain removes users’ setups.
Larger instances cost more.
Manual reminders aren’t reliable.
Idle shutdown stops apps automatically after a period of inactivity.
takeaway: Idle notebook spend → Studio idle shutdown.

question: A team builds custom inference containers in CodePipeline. Security requires that images with critical vulnerabilities in operating system or Python packages are blocked before deployment. Which service should the pipeline use to find the vulnerabilities?
options: Amazon Inspector
AWS Config
Amazon Macie
Amazon GuardDuty
explanations: Inspector scans container images, including OS and programming language packages, for known vulnerabilities.
Config evaluates resource configurations.
Macie finds sensitive data in S3.
GuardDuty detects threats from activity and logs.
takeaway: Vulnerabilities in images and packages → Amazon Inspector (ECR/CI-CD scanning).

question: A team’s AWS Lambda functions call Bedrock and process user input. Security wants automatic detection of code-level issues such as injection flaws and hard-coded credentials in the function code, as well as vulnerable dependencies. Which solution should the team use?
options: AWS X-Ray traces for the functions
Amazon Detective investigations
Amazon CodeGuru Reviewer for a new repository association
Amazon Inspector Lambda standard and code scanning
explanations: X-Ray traces requests; it doesn’t analyze code.
Detective investigates security findings.
CodeGuru Reviewer stopped accepting new customers in November 2025; AWS points to Inspector for code security.
Inspector scans Lambda dependencies and the function code for vulnerabilities such as injection and hard-coded secrets.
takeaway: Code and dependency scanning for Lambda → Inspector. (CodeGuru Reviewer is closed to new customers.)

question: A SageMaker AI execution role has the AmazonS3FullAccess policy. Training jobs for the fraud project need to read s3://ml-data/fraud/ and write to s3://ml-artifacts/fraud/. Which change applies least privilege?
options: Keep AmazonS3FullAccess and enable S3 Versioning on both buckets
Use the AWS account root user for training jobs
A policy with GetObject and PutObject on the two fraud prefixes
Attach AmazonSageMakerFullAccess instead
explanations: Versioning doesn’t limit access.
The root user should never run workloads.
Scoping actions and resources to the needed prefixes grants only the required access.
This is also broad.
takeaway: Least privilege → specific actions on specific resource prefixes.

question: Security requires that every SageMaker AI training job in the account runs inside approved private subnets. Data scientists create jobs from notebooks. How can the platform team enforce this?
options: Create a CloudWatch dashboard of training jobs
Enable VPC Flow Logs on the approved subnets
Deny CreateTrainingJob unless sagemaker:VpcSubnets matches
Ask data scientists to add a VPC configuration to every job
explanations: Dashboards don’t prevent noncompliant jobs.
Flow logs record traffic; they don’t enforce job settings.
SageMaker condition keys let IAM deny job creation that doesn’t use approved network settings.
A request isn’t enforcement.
takeaway: Enforce SageMaker settings → IAM condition keys (sagemaker:VpcSubnets, VolumeKmsKey, NetworkIsolation…).

question: A company has approved two foundation models in Amazon Bedrock for use by its applications. Developers must not invoke any other model. Which control should the ML engineer apply?
options: A CloudWatch alarm on invocations of other models
An S3 bucket policy on the training data
Allow bedrock:InvokeModel on the two model ARNs
A Bedrock guardrail with denied topics
explanations: An alarm detects use after the fact but doesn’t prevent it.
Bucket policies control S3 access.
Resource-level permissions in IAM limit invocation to specific models.
Guardrails filter content; they don’t restrict which models can be invoked.
takeaway: Limit which FMs can be called → IAM allow on specific model (or inference profile) ARNs.

question: A regulated company requires that data scientists can register models in SageMaker Model Registry but can’t approve them for production. Only the risk team may approve. How should the ML engineer implement this?
options: Store approved models in a separate S3 bucket
Turn off EventBridge events for the model registry in the account
Use a single IAM role for both teams and log approvals
Deny sagemaker:UpdateModelPackage to the data scientists’ role
explanations: Copying artifacts doesn’t control the registry status.
Disabling events doesn’t restrict who can approve.
Logging doesn’t prevent unauthorized approvals.
Approval status changes use UpdateModelPackage, so IAM can restrict who approves.
takeaway: Separation of duties in Model Registry → IAM controls on UpdateModelPackage.

question: An auditor asks who updated a production SageMaker AI endpoint last Tuesday and from which IP address. Which service provides this information?
options: Amazon Inspector
Amazon CloudWatch Metrics
AWS CloudTrail
AWS Compute Optimizer
explanations: Inspector reports vulnerabilities.
Metrics show performance numbers, not who made changes.
CloudTrail records API calls such as UpdateEndpoint with the identity, time, and source IP.
Compute Optimizer recommends instance sizes.
takeaway: Who did what, when, from where → CloudTrail.
